#2689. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2688. Sights and Sounds from San Antonio’s Gold Cup early round win at Sacramento

The Spurs put together two of their finest wins during SEGABAGA road victories over Sacramento and Portland. When the NBA schedule came out, my sister and I reviewed which game that we'd want to go to, saw the airfare prices to and from Austin and San Antonio…. and concluded Sacramento made the most sense for both of us.

Some observations from an excellent night in the Golden Center:

The best comp that I could come up with was slightly slower and less athletic Allen Iverson with Jamal Murray's shooting range on offense. However, he and the rest of his teammates seemed lost on most defensive possessions, which resulted in quite a few paint points for San Antonio.

Not only were there wide swaths of the lower bowl that had empty seats, but there was entire rows in the second level that lacked humans, too. Though the Kings did themselves no favors by falling and staying behind by nearly 20 points most of the game, the ambience itself lacked the fervor of past seasons.

Things I saw in-person that I haven't noticed on the good ole television:

Luke Kornet seems 15-20 pounds heavier than last season.

Domantas Sabonis tried a lot of his bull-in-a-china-shop physicality on Wembanyama in the paint – something that worked well in earlier seasons – but found it no longer works for him beyond occasionally.

Dylan Harper (see highlights below) looked like the best guard out there.

Wembanyama suffered his infamous face-plant during game 2 of the first-round series and turned his ankle rather gruesomely on Sabonis' closeout tonight – so maybe I shouldn't be going to these games in-person anymore.

I'm sad I didn't get video evidence of Jordan McLaughlin's dunk attempt in the second half. It was impressive!

Chik-Fil-A rewarded its fans with a free appetizer if a Spur missed two free throws in a row, and this might have been the biggest win tonight in Sacramento…. with the exception that fans had to claim their victory a) in the app and b) before 10 AM the next morning. I'll take breakfast tacos anytime.

What started as a bad omen but ultimately was a big nothing-burger: the Spurs' rim was being repaired for over 20 minutes right after Wembanyama finished his pre-game prep, affecting the tip-off by roughly 15 minutes or so. Right before the repairs took place, I was impressed with Wembanyama's (mostly) in-motion routine instead of just practicing stand-still jumpers:

The audacity AND accuracy of Stephon Castle's re-direction here to Vassell in the first period will likely put this in the season-ending highglight rankings:

Speaking of Devin, this literally was a logo jumper late in the first quarter:

There were shades of young Tony Parker on this and-1 by Harper.

About $90 million of salary failed to box out Wembanyama on this follow slam.

Castle – for my more mature audience – is like a latter generation Dominique Wilkins with these two-footed lob jams on anybody and everybody

These simple two-man motions with Victor and a guard and shooters on the other side are good enough to win a lot of regular season games while keeping both the big man and his teammates happy. Devin's shotmaking ability late in the shotclock is exquisite.

On a personal note, this was the first chance to watch the Spurs in-person with my sister and her two kids since my dad passed. During the last Spurs game here in Sacramento on March 17, my dad suffered his last major fall hurriedly trying to get into his TV room to watch the game. My Kings rep Gavin was kind enough to gift us post-game free throws, and Shirley credited my dad for willing her free throw into the net.

#2683. Austin Reaves steps up in Luka Doncic's absence to lead Lakers over Pistons

The Lakers' star guard banked in a fadeaway three-pointer. He nailed a clutch step-back with 44.5 seconds left. He trash-talked with fans.

Reaves embodied Doncic in almost every way Sunday, leading the Lakers to a 121-116 win over the Detroit Pistons as Doncic sat out with low back tightness. The Lakers replaced the guard averaging a league-high 40.1 points with Reaves' season-high 43 points, four assists and five rebounds.

The Lakers (9-2) needed every bit of Reaves' magic. Their 26-point second-quarter lead nearly evaporated under an avalanche of second-half turnovers and 55 combined points from Detroit bench guards Daniss Jenkins and Kevin Huerter.

Fresh off a max contract extension, Reaves has had a quiet yet ruthlessly efficient start to the year in Doncic's shadow. Doncic is getting most valuable player chants each time he steps to the free throw line. Reaves, averaging 25.3 points per game on 50.8% shooting from the field and 41.3% from three, has at times looked clumsy while getting comfortable with new teammates in the minutes without Doncic.

Read more: Luka Doncic's historic run jump-starts early MVP conversation

He looked comfortable in the starring role again Sunday. Reaves hit a seemingly impossible baseline fadeaway in the first quarter, flinging the ball almost over the backboard. When two fans sitting opposite the Lakers' bench started chirping at Reaves, he bent down, put his hands on his knees during a stoppage of play and talked directly at them for several seconds.

Doncic, dressed in black pants and a gray jacket, took it all in from the sideline.

"Sometimes when they're playing together, AR kind of has to take a secondary role," said center Walker Kessler, who had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including a clutch put-back, three-point play that put the Lakers up by eight with 2:15 remaining. "But I mean, as you can see now, he's very capable. He's a heck of a playmaker, heck of a scorer and a competitor."

On the front side of a back-to-back, Doncic missed his second game of the season with low back tightness, although Lakers coach JJ Redick said he didn't anticipate it to affect Doncic significantly throughout the season.

The Slovenian superstar is averaging a league-high 40.1 points per game, but Doncic was doing more than just scoring at rates not seen since Wilt Chamberlain. His estimated on/off of 37.7 — the difference between the Lakers' net rating when he was on the court compared to off — was the second-highest in the league, following only Victor Wembanyama's 41.5. In addition to having the highest scoring average through nine games since Chamberlain, Doncic is the team's second-leading rebounder at 7.8 per game and is second with 1.7 steals.

Austin Reaves goes to the basket against Pistons guard Kevin Huerter in the second half Sunday. (Duane Burleson / Associated Press)

But the Lakers already showed they could compete without Doncic this season. They dominated the Clippers on Oct. 28 when he was sidelined, also with back tightness.

Just as they did against the Clippers, the Lakers needed contributions from everyone. Ziaire Williams hit four three-pointers and finished with 17 points. Collin Sexton, serving as the Lakers' second ball-handler, had 17 points on five-of-10 shooting.

Jarred Vanderbilt's energetic six rebounds, two assists and one block in less than six minutes during the first quarter helped lift the Lakers to a 26-point lead early in the second.

The Pistons, playing without All-NBA center Jalen Duren (hamstring), didn't get their first points from star point guard Cade Cunningham until early in the third quarter. Instead, Jenkins nearly mounted the comeback on his own.

Jenkins, a familiar Lakers foe who scored 30 points in Detroit's win over the Lakers here last year, scored 22 points of his career-high 31 in the first half, cutting the Lakers' 26-point lead to 13 by halftime. He drained a three-pointer at the buzzer that injected life into the antsy home crowd. The Lakers, who have benefited from two halftime buzzer-beating heaves from Doncic this season, know what it's like to be on the other side of that momentum swing.

Read more: Swanson: Luka Doncic can lead Lakers to a title, but only if his teammates pull their weight

Pistons fans banging inflatable thunder sticks erupted in the third quarter as Detroit ripped off an 11-0 run to close the lead to three with 1:03 remaining in the quarter. The Lakers, playing with Sexton as their primary ballhandler during the stretch, had four turnovers during the drought, including a shot clock violation after a timeout.

Reaves rested from the sideline during the slide, but Redick stayed committed to the pre-determined rotation matrix to ensure star players get their necessary breaks.

"If you start just overreacting in-game and saying 'I gotta get this guy back in, I gotta get this guy back in,' it's just chaos," Redick said. "And we're trying to create consistency for our players."

Redick called Reaves "Mr. Consistency" earlier this season. He had 13 points in the third quarter, including five straight on difficult fadeway jumpers that pushed the lead to 17 with 6:41 to go in the third. After his step-back three from the wing kissed off the glass and rattled through the rim, Reaves shrugged.

"It was 100% lucky," said Reaves, who called the daring step-back the type of ill-advised shot Doncic would attempt.

Reaves shot Doncic's shots then talked Doncic's talk. After hitting the dagger shot to put the Lakers up by eight with 44.5 seconds left, Reaves turned and waved goodbye directly to the two fans sitting courtside.

#2681. Mitch Albom: Lions won't have many easy wins. But does it matter?

Dan Campbell knew what this was by halftime. He barked it into the CBS cameras.

"We gotta calm down … and then we GOTTA GO! We can't be messing around!"

Exactly. When playing a team that is 1-6, a good team often finds itself inexplicably fumbling and bumbling. It's like when you can't get that first piece of plastic to peel off the box. You start normal, then you try your fingernails, then you get frustrated, and you wind up screaming to yourself, "Why is this so damn hard?"

That was the Detroit Lions for much of Sunday's game in Miami against the low-win but high-effort Dolphins. Detroit's first drive used up nearly seven minutes but ended with a sack of Jared Goff on third-and-goal. A field goal had to suffice.

Their second drive ended in an interception, when Goff was pressured and a defender hit his arm as he tried to pass.

Their fourth drive, after starting with great field position, fizzled when Jahmyr Gibbs was yanked down twice in a row for thre- yard losses and Goff was pressured into a scramble.

The NFL's highest-flying offense was hovering very close to the ground.

Fortunately, Miami couldn't take advantage. They punted twice, notched a field goal, and wasted an 11-play drive with a doink off the uprights by their kicker, Zane Gonzalez.

Halftime ended at Lions 6, Miami 3. Which is what led Campbell to his "we can't be messing around" critique, which I'm sure he delivered in the locker room with a fervor that would have scared the average TV viewer.

And eventually, they did stop messing around. And they finally brought home a 19-9 win that may have certain critics attacking them for, well, not being able to get the plastic off a box faster than that.

[ LIVE REACTIONS: Make the "Freep Sports Show" your go-to Detroit/Michigan sports podcast, available anywhere you listen (Apple or Spotify). Join us live on YouTube after every Lions game. ]

Remember, this is a team coming off an emotional injury to one of their most beloved and important players, linebacker Jack Campbell. It swirled around practice all week. When one football player sees another football player face down and not moving, it stays with them − believe me. Dealing with Campbell's health uncertainly, then getting a positive message from him midweek, then having to focus on an opponent that should be easy to beat ... well, all that is a perfect recipe for the old trap game, where you go home shaking your head saying, "How did we lose to them?"

That didn't happen Sunday against the Dolphins, and the Lions first deserve credit for that. Four plays into the second half, safety Chuck Clark snagged a Malik Willis pass and turned into a running back, cutting angles and using blocks. He returned the ball 34 yards to the Miami 26. For a maligned secondary, it was a sweet moment and a turnaround, one that invoked Campbell's "no more messing around."

LIONS GRADES: High marks for defense in emotional win over Dolphins

The Lions scored points on their ensuring drive, and their next drive, and their next, and Jared Goff, on a subpar day, hit just enough of a string of big passes. And Jahmyr Gibbs, on a subpar day, scooted past everyone for an eight-yard TD, the only touchdown in the game. And Jake Bates, after a subpar kickoff that was like watching a blimp go down, made all four field goal attempts. And next thing you knew, the Lions had the ball and a 19-9 lead. All they had to do was keep possession, and they did, with Goff executing a quarterback sneak on a fourth-and-1 with under two minutes to play – Detroit's fourth out of four fourth down tries.

"I thought [Miami] rushed really well and tackled really well," said Goff in the postgame press conference when asked about Detroit sluggish offense. "We certainly had our opportunities to blow it open a little bit earlier than that and didn't take advantage of them. Some self-inflicted wounds, some penalties pre-snap. … It took us a minute to get going there, obviously, but when we did, we did enough to win."

Or as Campbell put it to the media, more succinctly: "It took us a minute to get in it."

Here's the other thing, folks: This year's Lions are not complete enough, deep enough, or healthy enough to go on some win-every-game-by-20-or-more streak. There are holes that spring in the boat on a weekly basis. On Sunday, the offensive line, which had been a strong point earlier in the year, was continuously overrun by Miami's average defense. The Dolphins sacked Goff three times in the first half, pressured him into one interception and harassed him into bad passes or throwaways all day.

That same offensive line couldn't open holes for Detroit's best weapon, Gibbs, who was consistently dragged down and had only one big escape burst for 16 yards. Take that away, and Gibbs averaged 3 yards a carry and a total of 74 yards, which is OK for mortals, but not for Superman.

Rookie tackle Blake Miller had a rough game, getting beat on defenders coming for Goff. Miles Frazier was a surprise starter in place of Christian Mahogany. Cade Mays was out. They say the most important part of an effective offensive line is consistency and familiarity. Detroit doesn't have that luxury right now.

LIONS WINNERS AND LOSERS: Kelvin Sheppard has defense humming

And while the defense was stellar in keeping the Dolphins out of the end zone and made the big plays late, which is what winning teams do, the Lions can't count on every opponent drawing 11 penalties for 87 yards, most of which sent the Miami offense backwards.

The fact is, every week will be a challenge for these Lions – now minus their defensive leader, Campbell.

The other fact is they have risen to the challenge now, six out of eight times.

"It's been six different ways [of winning] and four in a row now in four different ways," Goff said. "That's the hallmark of a good team, when you're able to find different ways to win repeatedly."

Meanwhile, the Lions do have something unique. There was a locker set for Jack Campbell in their locker room in Miami. And according to Dan Campbell, "That locker's travelling."

Don't downplay that. Many a team has used a fallen teammate as rocket fuel for the season, and the Lions may do the same. Just don't expect it to be easy against the weaker teams, any more than you expect to be dominated by the stronger ones.

Sometimes winning games is just remembering to do as Campbell said: Calm down, get going and stop messing around. Which is why you get that plastic off the box eventually, even if, as with Sunday's game, it seems like it shouldn't have been that hard.

#2680. Sunday Night Football: Bears overcome five giveaways, beat Bucs 27-24

It was a wild one in Chicago, but the Bears were able to pull out a 27-24 victory over the Buccaneers and move to 7-2 on the season.

Caleb Williams and the Bears' offense started out white hot, but an interception midway through the second quarter threw off the unit for nearly the rest of the night. Williams ended up tossing four interceptions — the most in a single game he's had in his college or pro career.

But even with five giveaways — Luther Burden also had a fumble in the fourth quarter — the Buccaneers scored just 10 points off of them. Tampa Bay couldn't turn a blocked punt into points either, despite getting the ball at midfield.

Chicago began the game with a 14-0 lead, as Williams tossed touchdowns to Rome Odunze and Burden. The Buccaneers got on the board with Chase McLaughlin's 27-yard field goal in the second quarter before Cairo Santos hit from 25 yards to make the score 17-3 with 3:02 left in the half. McLaughlin drilled a 21-yard field goal to end the half, with Bucs head coach Todd Bowles explaining in his halftime interview on the NBC broadcast that he felt his team could score to start the third quarter.

That turned into reality, as Bucky Irving scored a 2-yard touchdown to cap Tampa Bay's opening drive in the second half, narrowing Chicago's lead to 17-13.

While Williams threw his fourth interception, Baker Mayfield then threw a pick of his own to Jaylon Johnson, who returned it 67 yards for a touchdown.

McLaughlin again made it a one-possession game with a 35-yard field goal with 11:24 in the fourth quarter. Then Burden's fumble gave the Buccaneers the opportunity to tie it deep in Bears territory, with Irving scoring on a 6-yard run. Mayfield made the two-point conversion successful by scrambling up the middle to the end zone.

But even with the offensive challenges, the Bears got the play they needed to win it. Williams connected with Colton Loveland for a 38-yard pass all the way down to the Tampa Bay 16.

After running time off the clock, Santos sent the ball through the uprights as the fourth quarter expired for a 38-yard, game-winning field goal.

Williams finished the contest 22-of-37 for 279 yards with two touchdowns and four picks. Burden led with seven catches for 97 yards with a TD. He had to be examined in the sideline medical tent after his fumble in the fourth quarter and was subsequently taken back to the locker room for further evaluation.

Mayfield finished 18-of-32 for 243 yards with two picks. Irving had 97 yards on 20 carries with two TDs, plus four catches for 28 yards.

With the win, the Bears are 7-2 in the league's best division — as all teams in the NFC North have at least six wins. Chicago will be on its bye in Week 10 before hosting the Saints in Week 11.

At 3-6, the Buccaneers will also be on their bye in Week 10. They'll look to get back on track on the road against the Lions in Week 11.

#2679. Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren't about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit's point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons' rotation this season. In a game where Detroit's entire backcourt didn't really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he'd be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he's hitting 40% from deep this season.

Detroit's starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain't pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it's the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it's two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It's an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers' big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion's share of the blame goes to Collins. He's been quite bad all season, and it's getting less clear by the day how he's going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don't think he's ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn't surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he'd never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, "This is not going to happen."

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He's got scoring in his blood, and he's more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard's body. He's got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he's better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he's not running the offense.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

#2674. What Nique Clifford to the Thunder means for the Spurs

The Thunder and the Kings completed an early-season trade that surprised most observers. Oklahoma City acquired second-year player Nique Clifford from Sacramento in exchange for two second-round picks, as first reported by ESPN's Shams Charania.

The trade is strange from the Kings' side, and we'll get to it. As far as the Spurs are concerned, however, the biggest impact comes from the Thunder once again getting cost-controlled, young talent for middling draft assets to bolster their depth in the present and the near future. Let's start there.

First things first: Clifford is not Jared McCain. All they have in common is that they were both second-year players whose previous teams gave up on them, and they were both traded to Oklahoma City for two second-rounders. The main difference between the two is that McCain was so impressive to start his first season in Philadelphia that he was the frontrunner for Rookie of the Year for a while, before getting hurt. Clifford, who entered the league at 23 years of age, had an acceptable but unimpressive first season for a horrible Kings team. The McCain trade was a bigger deal than this one at the time, and McCain's impact will likely be bigger than Clifford's in the future.

With that out of the way, it's still a good move for Oklahoma City, as they needed depth at the wing after losing Jalen Williams and likely Cason Wallace for the rest of the season. Clifford is 6'5 with a 6'8 wingspan, a jack-of-all-trades player who can fill in the gaps in lineups. He's someone who, in theory, can contribute in many different ways, which is always helpful for good teams that already have elite scorers and creators in place and can use guys who won't demand too many touches. There's a really good chance he thrives as a secondary or tertiary creator in Oklahoma City while providing solid defense. Considering what it took to get him, he's not a bad stopgap.

The real impact this trade could have, however, is on the future affordability of an increasingly expensive Thunder roster. Clifford is almost certainly not good enough to give OKC even half of the production of either of their starting wings who are out with injury, but he could be a solid depth piece going forward. He's in the second year of a very cheap rookie deal, so Sam Presti could get almost three years of production out of him on a cost-controlled contract, which means that when everyone returns, the Thunder could have both top talent and depth, which is becoming increasingly hard to do in the apron era.

By essentially re-drafting guys using second-round picks, OKC is building a pipeline of young talent to replace their own misses in talent evaluation and veterans who become too expensive.

That's bad news for every Western Conference team, including the Spurs.

Both analysts and people on social media are mocking the Kings for trading a first-rounder to OKC to select Clifford in the 2025 draft only to, just after a season and change, trade him to the Thunder for two seconds. It's a funny sequence of events from a poorly run franchise, so the jokes are understandable, but, in reality, it isn't as bad as it might seem at first glance.

First, the first-round pick the Kings traded to get Clifford was the Spurs' 2027 pick that they got in the De'Aaron Fox trade. The pick will likely be in the late 20s. Moving that asset for a pick of similar value (Clifford was selected 24th overall) was not necessarily a terrible idea by the Kings at the time, since they clearly liked Nique then. And cutting your losses if you think you made a mistake drafting someone is better than falling for the sunk-cost fallacy and holding on even after you've concluded the player just isn't good. Sacramento actually had to send out a second-round pick to shed former lottery pick Devin Carter Jr.'s salary, so they were probably trying to avoid doing the same with Clifford, who was out of the rotation.

But there might be an explanation for the trade that doesn't involve Sacramento thinking Clifford is a bust: the new lottery rules put the Kings in a bad position, and the move was a way to salvage something.

Starting next draft, the teams with the bottom three records will be in the relegation zone and will actually get worse odds of getting the top pick than a non-playoff team with a better record. The entire point of the change was to make sure coaches didn't just sit their veterans with fake injuries to tank as hard as they could while trotting out lineups featuring players who didn't belong in the NBA. It's entirely possible that the Kings felt like they needed to put guys on the floor who could lift them to at least the fourth-worst record, and thought Clifford was not one of them. Not yet, at least. At that point, trading him before he loses all value after being buried on the bench makes sense.

The Kings' reputation is so bad that explaining the move this way might seem too charitable, especially since even while playing their veterans, they are 1-8 and are a likely bottom-three team. Whether this specific move by this specific franchise is smart remains to be seen, but it wouldn't be shocking to see more mediocre-to-bad teams with young players that need developmental minutes that just aren't there moving on quickly while trying to get some value back.

If that's the case, contenders should be on the lookout for re-drafting opportunities, and Brian Wright should be ready to pounce if someone he likes becomes available.

#2669. Best division ever? How NFC North is on pace to make history in 2026

Best division ever? How NFC North is on pace to make history in 2026 originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Bears found a way to win on Sunday night, overcoming five turnovers to defeat the Buccaneers 27-24, but they certainly aren't alone in the NFC North.

The Packers and Lions both continued their winning ways on Sunday, and, until Monday at least, none of those three teams can say they only one loss like the Vikings do.

All four NFC North teams will enter Week 10 in the playoff picture. While head-to-head matchups might hurt the division's chances of getting every team into the playoffs, it's becoming clear these four teams are in a class of their own as a group.

Here's a look at how the NFC North could be headed for uncharted territory.

MORE: Which NFL trade candidates boosted - or hurt - their stocks in Week 9?

The NFC North is now 25-8 (.757) through nearly nine weeks, with five of those eight losses simply coming against one another. NFC North teams are 20-3 in non-divisional games.

Here are the standings after Sunday night, with the Vikings still to play on Monday:

Every team in the division is at least three games over .500, meaning the Packers are in last place at 6-3. In the NFC North, for comparison, the 3-5 Panthers lead the division.

The Bears have had a hard time gaining ground during the four-game win streak because of all of the success around them, but a Vikings loss to the Bills on Monday night would rocket Chicago into first place.

MORE:4 quarterbacks who boosted their early MVP cases in Week 9

When it comes to divisions, there are two distinct periods in the NFL: pre-2002, when divisions were larger than four teams, and 2002-present, when all divisions have been comprised of four teams.

The overall records within divisions were more even before 2002 because more teams were in each. Since 2002, the best record for a division belongs to the 2024 NFC North, which saw teams go a combined 45-23 (.662) as the Lions went 15-2, Vikings went 14-3, Packers went 11-6 and Bears went 7-10. Two years earlier, in the NFC East went a combined 43-23-2, sending three teams to the playoffs.

So far, the NFC North is on track to break its own record in 2026. At 25-8 (.757), every team is at least three games above .500 and their combined record would have to be 20-15 the rest of the way to match the 2024 mark.

There are still seven divisional games on the docket in the NFC North, so the division will have at least 15 losses. If these four teams can keep it to only eight additional losses, the division will tie its own record from 2002.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

The Diamondbacks are expected to listen to offers for second baseman Ketel Marte, reports the Arizona Republic. The D-backs entertained trade offers last offseason, but were unable to find a match. Marte has full no-trade protection and can direct where he lands, if he wants to leave Arizona at all. His desire to change teams is unknown.

Marte, 33, had a down year by his standards in 2026. He also went AWOL in August, prompting the D-backs to put him on the restricted list. Manager Torey Lovullo later revealed it was the fourth straight season Marte missed a game without permission. Beyond the on-field fit, teams will have to weigh the potential clubhouse impact and headaches.

The Seibu Lions in Japan will make right-hander Kaima Taira available to MLB teams via the posting system this offseason, the team announced Friday. The posting is expected to be made official in the coming days. Once that happens, Taira will have 45 days to negotiate and sign with an MLB team, otherwise he will return to Japan in 2027.

We ranked Taira as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason. Here's our write-up:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man.

Taira, 27 next month, threw 146 innings with a 1.36 ERA and 141 strikeouts this past season. He actually had higher ERAs as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, though he has been excellent throughout his career in Japan, and has the bat-missing power stuff that tends to translate well to MLB. Taira figures to be highly sought after in the coming weeks.

The trading season resumed Thursday and the Red Sox were involved in the offseason's first two trades. First, they sent utility man Nate Eaton to the Athletics for minor-league righty Jareth Rayo, the team announced. The A's recently named former Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith their new president of baseball operations. His first move was bringing in Eaton, a player he's presumably familiar with given their overlapping time in Boston.

Next, the Red Sox traded infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, the team announced. Cheng, 25, is a glove-first utility man who appeared in 14 games with Boston this past season. Both the Cheng and Eaton trades open up 40-man roster spots for the Red Sox, who still must open three more spots to accommodate their seven players on the 60-day injured list. They must be activated no later than this coming Monday.

#2664. On the future of the NBA in Mexico, from the Global Games to a franchise

MEXICO CITY: No city outside the United States or Canada has hosted more regular season NBA games than Mexico City. So it should come as no surprise that the annual tilts held in the Mexican capital are the frequent backdrop for rumbles about the league setting up shop on a more permanent basis in the largest metropolis on the continent.

In recent years, however, the league making a return to the Pacific Northwest to put a new team back in Seattle, Washington along with a new team in Las Vegas, Nevada seemed a fait accompli, and with it, hope for an NBA team in the city faded. But before the start of the 2026 season, it was announced at an NBA Board of Governor's meeting that Mexico City was back in the mix with a potential ownership group and arena district lined up. Still, the Mexico City Game has been and will likely remain the gem in the crown of the league that is their Global Games series, a yearly accomplishment on its own signifying the nascent talent and fandom of Latin America now percolating into the league's ranks.

To learn more, the Rookie Wire caught up with NBA Latin America and Canada Head of Operations Raul Zarraga ahead of the 2026 Mexico City Game between the Denver Nuggets and Indiana Pacers. From the state of the Association in Mexico, and what the future of Mexico City Games and NBA expansion in the region might look like, our conversation covered the gamut and then some.

This interview has been lightly edited for the purposes of clarity and brevity.

Raul Zarraga: Of course. The Global Game – it's a great opportunity for us. You have this life experience for fans and partners and everyone in the community, and all the people enjoying the game. Keep in mind that less than one percent of people around the world have the opportunity to be in-person for a regular season NBA game. And that's why it's very important for us to give a piece of that action to all the fans in Mexico. I wish we could have many more games available for fans. But we are very happy with the experience so far.

It's sold out in a couple of days. The two amazing teams, we're really looking forward to (having them) here: the Pacers and the Nuggets. The Pacers for the first time, the Nuggets the second, and it's a whole celebration together, a unique way to mix two very important components: entertainment and the culture. Something that the fans are really looking for, regardless if they are core, casual, (or) curious fans of our 30 million fans (in Latin America), this is a great opportunity to enjoy the NBA. And we have other assets at the Capitanes (Mexico City's G League team) as well for live experiences. So we have this regular season (game), and then we tip off the season for Capitanes for 21 games of regular season happening here.

So, it's a great momentum for players, for legends, for the fans, for the community, for the partners, for the people watching the game through the different kind of content channel, the distribution channels, and again, as I said, it's just the beginning of an amazing season that is ahead of us this 2026.

RZ: First of all, thank you for recognizing! I would say it's a combination of teamwork, talent, and people that has been here. This is my game No. 18 or 19, if I'm not mistaken. I've been 18 years in the league, so around that. And I love to see many of the same faces after all these years. It's expertise together with new talent helping us to streamline processes with different technologies. Even AI, all this new technology that helps to organize and communicate things in a better, more efficient way.

The global mindset of teams and players and staff and all the people around the game (too). They've been traveling to China and then Europe, or they go to Europe and Latin America, Brazil, or Canada. This mindset of understanding the culture is very important. When we have, for instance, training presentations to the teams, to the staff, we have this group that helps people to understand the local culture, the way that we do things here in Mexico as a country, and that helps the staff to understand the best way to move around.

It helps also to understand how they can approach different kind of requests. That's the mindset of the global entity. We're a global league that really understands the market, and we spend a lot of time understanding the local dynamic to make sure that we keep learning to make the best possible experience for our three main audiences: fans, partners, and of course, for the teams. Partners as you, as the media, because we consider media as a partner helping us to communicate the things that we want to communicate, and the fans want to listen.

RZ: Thank you for that comparison. The All-Stars, of course, are the best of the best, but I would say that the experience (is) for everyone. We have the same people organizing the All Star Game here in different ways. Partner activation, operations, the whole operation of the arena, that the security team, the basketball operations team, all of them. It is kind of a celebration as well.

Of course, All-Star is a celebration, and it's a very important opportunity to be a fan, to watch the teams, the players, to enjoy life as well. The experience we have learned from All-Star could be also translated here to different fan activations, and you've been at the arena. You've been at concourse level. (There's) that kind of fun day, fun fest we organized three hours before the tip-off of the game.

Every market has a different way to celebrate the game. All-Star for sure is an iconic experience ... but here we have the same kind of (experience) for our local fan base, (to) celebrate with fans, with content creators. For instance, we are we are doing something unique this year, a content creators club, bringing creators from different parts of Canada, Brazil, of course Mexico, and give them access to share, communicate, to tell the people what is going on with a different kind of language many fans are using right now, especially with the NBA. We have 30 million fans and around 25 percent are Gen Z fans, people consuming content all day on all kinds of mobile devices ... this format helps to communicate to them in a different way.

The Game starts when we do the announcement, and start doing promotions ... we broke the record with people registered in the system to for pre-sale (tickets). The Pacers will be having ... special merchandise around Día de Muertos. Día de Muertos, for instance, is a great way to combine culture and entertainment for fans here and for the people visiting us from different countries.

RZ: Putting aside the other components about the cup and everything, no, not at this moment. Ideas are floating about the different things that we could do here. But at this point, there are no plans to have any summer league or All-Star game here in Mexico. We definitely have the market. It's the largest city in North America. It has the time zone, the infrastructure, the fan base here to have to do many things and really grow, keep growing our footprint in the market.

Right now, our focus is based on three main components: Participation, live experience, and availability of our of content. We have content, of course, our games, video, and ESPN. We have around eight million followers in Mexico and 30 million followers in Latin America, having around just Mexico 200 million interactions on social media and 700 million in Latin America during the past season. So our focus right now is also making sure that the NBA is available in any of its formats to the fans.

RZ: Everything remains as the commissioner mentioned before us up to date. We've been focused on growing the fan base here as one of the main strategies. Taking into consideration, of course, that basketball is the second most practiced team sport here in Mexico, and of course, more basketball courts than any other sport.

The official version has been already shared by Adam (Silver), and it's going to remain the same until the NBA decides something different. The arena is an amazing arena to keep having our regular season games in. it's actually so good that Capitanes are playing there as well. We have a great relationship with Zignia, and our focus remains there.

RZ: Because of the time time zone for sure, proximity. Even the Hispanic market as well. The Hispanic market, as you know, is huge in the U.S. and that helps a lot ... And it's part of the global offer that we have for fans and partners. Part of that, for instance, is Prime Video (of) Mexico, Brazil. Latin America was one of the first regions starting streaming games of Prime Video.

And that's because we are very close, of course, and we have the same time zones in many of the games, and it's very helpful ... we're a global entity, and have a footprint around all the world: China, India, Africa, Europe, Canada, and Latin America. We have players, legends, we have a basketball framework.

RZ: We understand Latin America is a very good opportunity to expand our interaction with authorities. We have a great relationship with FIBA Americas, and Basketball Without Borders is a great example. We constantly do this camp in Latin America, with them to identify the talent that in the future could be there. Several players that are currently at the NBA started there, (like) someone from the academy in San Luis Potosí, Benedict Mathurin. He used to play for the Pacers. So, talent has been promoted and identified. It's not easy to be in the NBA, as we all know.

It's a very, very competitive environment for any player. But I can tell you that our basketball programs remain one of the most important initiatives that we keep building all around the region. Talking to trainers, coaches, physical educators, kids, to communities to ensure that they can have the best possible basketball infrastructure to keep playing the game, whether it is something that in the future could be translated to a player, to the Capitanes, or to any other league in the market that they are operating.

We are currently not focused on replicating something that has been done in Africa or in Europe here in Latin America. Because we are focused on the things that I previously mentioned. The future, we're really optimistic about the things that we can keep doing to grow our fan base, and of course, the opportunity for the people to play basketball.

RZ: I remember the tip off when I was in Memphis, if I'm not mistaken, for their first game. We were all trying to understand (their role), the ownership group, the players, us, everything. Now that I see the team, the way that they are assembled, the way they played the previous season, getting into the playoffs, the way they broke the record of (G League) attendance. It was a huge, an amazing experience. So like everything, it takes time to understand the role that they have.

Now, I see a very solid group of people dedicated to make the best possible team that they can, including the ownership group ... and a group of young entrepreneurs really looking to keep growing this unique project that they have, being the first (non-US) expansion that the G League has had besides in Canada ... it's just such a unique thing. It's an iconic component of our footprint here in Mexico. And I see that evolution with the fans as well.

I see the classic cheer of Capitanes. The partners as well, ESPN broadcasting the games. Viewership also keeps increasing. The level of interaction, the talent pipeline, and when you are in the game and you see people precisely having this kind of experience for 21 games in regular season, it's something that definitely has grown in all the simple metrics – audience, attendance, merchandising, even participation. They have basketball schools in Mexico City promoting the brand and the opportunity for them to have more fans.

This article originally appeared on Rookie Wire: On the future of the NBA in Mexico, from the Global Games to a franchise

#2663. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

#2662. "He won't be able to leave me out next time!" - Raum sends message to Klopp

RB Leipzig enjoyed a convincing 5-2 victory over FC Augsburg, but David Raum had an additional reason to celebrate. After being left out of Jürgen Klopp's latest Germany squad, the defender used his goal to send a message and vowed to make the national team coach reconsider his decision.

The Leipzig defender admitted that his goal against Augsburg carried some extra motivation after weeks of speculation and media coverage surrounding his national team future.

"There was a little bit of frustration behind the goal. A lot has been written in the media over the past few weeks, which, to put it bluntly, has really annoyed me. So I responded with my goal," Raum explained.

The defender also revealed that he had spoken directly with Klopp following the squad announcement. Despite disagreeing with the decision, Raum emphasised that he respects the national team coach's choice.

"Klopp called me. A lot of newspapers had already written various things about what he supposedly said. I respect his decision, and I told him that. After being involved for a long time, this is the first time I've been left out in a while. I also told him that I'll respond with my performances so that next time he won't be able to leave me out."

Raum added that he wished Klopp and the national team success, stressing that he wants Germany to move forward and become a team the country can be proud of. He also made clear that he intends to contribute again in the future.

Finally, the 28-year-old praised teammate Brajan Gruda, who was included in the latest Germany squad.

"Brajan showed today why he fully deserves his place in the national team. He played brilliantly and has earned it. He should enjoy the experience and perform for Germany just as well as he does here."

#2659. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. #2655. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

PCA, who also won a Gold Glove in 2025 and is expected to be named the NL MVP in 2026, was the best defender in baseball this past season based on both the numbers and the eye test.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Crow-Armstrong's +26 FRV is the fifth best in a single season since FRV launched in 2016 and the second best by a non-catcher, trailing only Nick Ahmed's +28 FRV season at shortstop in 2018.

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. Now the outfield spots are broken down into left field, center field, and right field.

Winners are determined through manager/coach voting (75%) and a statistical component (25%). Team employees can not vote for their own players.

While MLB announced "finalists" for each Gold Glove a few weeks back, remember that the voting was already complete and those finalists were simply the top three vote-getters at each position. #2650. UCF prevails in yet another off-the-rails finish, defeating Kansas, 33-32

UCF and chaotic, seemingly inexplicable finishes have become quite the pairing this season.

Two weeks after knocking off BYU in perhaps the wildest ending of the college football season, the Knights found themselves in another crunch time thriller Saturday, this time on the road at Kansas.

For most of the contest, UCF appeared on track to secure its first comfortable victory in Big 12 play. The Knights built a 26-7 lead by the 9:52 mark of the third quarter, seemingly having solved the Jayhawks on both sides of the ball. But their next two possessions went nowhere, producing consecutive three-and-outs that combined for -6 yards. That sudden offensive futility left the door ajar for a Kansas comeback, and the Jayhawks capitalized with two-straight touchdown drives and a field goal to trim the deficit to 26-24.

Then, following a spectacular punt by Atticus Bertrams, Kansas regained possession at its own 5-yard line with 2:27 remaining, needing just a field goal to complete the program's largest comeback since 2010. Somehow, the Jayhawks crammed 11 plays and 95 yards into 81 seconds, capping the clutch drive with a Dylan Edwards touchdown run with 1:06 remaining, catapulting Kansas ahead 32-26.

But the scoring drive was so quick that it granted UCF 66 seconds of opportunity while armed with two timeouts. The drive did not start in promising fashion as the Knights opened the drive with several misfires. But quarterback Alonza Barnett III — making his first start since suffering a hamstring injury in Week 2 — caught fire, jumpstarting the offense with a 20-yard completion to Tyren Hornes on 3rd-and-10. Then he hit Chase Hinshaw for another 20 and Josh Derry for a 19-yar pickup, positioning UCF 15 yards away from the end zone with 13 seconds remaining.

Then, the Knights went for the punishing blow. Barnett lofted a pass toward the back of the end zone, where Derry made a juggling grab while falling backward. The official initially threw his hands up to signal touchdown, but the replay review showed Derry had not secured possession before landing out of bounds. The call was overturned, leaving UCF eight seconds to work with.

The next attempt didn't produce a touchdown, but it still benefited the Knights. They drew a pass interference penalty, advancing the ball from the 15-yard line to the 6, giving UCF one more opportunity to reclaim the victory.

On the deciding play, Barnett kept his eyes to the left from the snap, patiently waiting for tight end Caden Piening to break toward the boundary. Barnett fired the pass, and Piening made a diving catch right before the sideline. The official emphatically raised both arms to the sky to signal a UCF touchdown, but once again, the Knights' fate rested with the replay officials.

Multiple angle played on the stadium scoreboard and ESPN2 broadcast as review seemingly lasted an hour for the anxious fans in Lawrence and the players on both sidelines. After several minutes of discussion, the replay center ruled there was no evidence to overturn the initial ruling to an incompletion. Touchdown, UCF.

With the game deadlocked at 32-32, UCF trotted out kicker Will Stone for the all-important extra point. But the probable kick wasn't necessarily a given as Stone missed his first extra point of the evening. However, through the added pressure, the senior drilled it, allowing the Knights to undo Kansas' dramatic comeback and escape Lawrence, 33-32.

The 33 points marked UCF's highest scoring output in regulation in Big 12 play this season. Barnett's return provided the offense a significant spark, as the James Madison transfer finished with 251 passing yards and two touchdowns, while extending plays with 36 yards as a rusher. Derry served as his top target, generating a season-high 143 yards on eight catches, including the crucial 19-yard reception that set up UCF in the red zone on the game-winning drive.

When Stone's extra point split the uprights, it was more than just one emotional win. It signified the end of a troubling trend as the Knights ended their 12-game road losing streak, capturing their first win away from home since Sept. 14, 2024 when they overcame a 21-point deficit at TCU.

UCF (5-4, 3-3 Big 12) matched its win total from the 2025 season by prevailing in Lawrence. Now, the Knights will have three chances to clinch bowl eligibility during the final month of the regular season with Arizona State, Iowa State, and Colorado looming on the schedule — three opponents currently below .500.

UCF has yet to post a winning season since joining the Big 12 in 2023. But after ending up on the right side of another improbable finish, the "Cardiac Knights" have given themselves a legitimate chance to change that. And after the BYU and Kansas games, who knows what chaos may unfold along the way?

#2643. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

Arguably the best pitcher in baseball is up for grabs this winter. Tarik Skubal is a free agent for the 2026-27 MLB offseason, easily the top available on the market, and every team should be trying to earn his services. But will they? Almost certainly not.

The 29-year-old southpaw spent the first six years of his major-league career with the Detroit Tigers before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. He won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and earned MVP votes in both seasons. He's likely to become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history both in total value and AAV.

Of course, the giant flashing sign floating above all of this is the expiring CBA, which will run out at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, after which the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. Over the summer, the league proposed limiting free agency contracts, an offer that the players' union quickly disavowed, and the owners' demand for a salary cap is the underlying throughline of every negotiation. Perhaps that means Skubal will rush to sign on the dotted line before new rules are in place. Perhaps that means teams will wait out the negotiations until they know how much they have to spend -- and how they'll be punished if they do so.

Regardless, CBS Sports' MLB experts, three people who are very much not involved in contract negotiations, have gathered to predict where Skubal lands by the time Opening Day rolls around.

Mike Axisa: I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction.

Dayn Perry: I'll say the Mets top all offers by a margin sufficient to overcome their lack of appeal compared to the usual suspects (meaning, mostly, the Dodgers). They definitely need a stabilizing force in the rotation outside of Nolan McLean, and they also need a vibes shift after the deeply disappointing 2026 campaign. Landing the biggest fish of all on the market would provide all that and meet a clear need. The Mets will already be rebound candidates in 2027, and signing the likes of Skubal would position them as contenders. Obviously, the structure of the next CBA has bearing here, but maybe this all comes together before the lockout shuts it all down for an indeterminate period of time.

Matt Snyder: I'll go with the easy and obvious answer and say the Dodgers. I don't think the owners win the fight for a salary cap, but there'll be enough push from the Dodgers' end before the CBA talks shut down free agency to snatch up all the talent they can to get his contract grandfathered before a new agreement.
